entries.063b0f570b96b6d2641d31f8ab00d16f5e0a8d95: <div sID="gen9968" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="30" osisID="Job.30" sID="Job.30"/> <div eID="gen9968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9970" type="x-p"/> It is a melancholy "But now" which this chapter begins with. Adversity is here described as much to the life as prosperity was in the foregoing chapter, and the height of that did but increase the depth of this. God sets the one over-against the other, and so did Job, that his afflictions might appear the more grievous, and consequently his case the more pitiable. I. He had lived in great honour, but now he had fallen into disgrace, and was as much vilified, even by the meanest, as ever he had been magnified by the greatest; this he insists much on, <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. He had had much inward comfort and delight, but now he was a terror and burden to himself (<reference osisRef="Job.30.15-Job.30.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>) and overwhelmed with sorrow, <reference osisRef="Job.30.28-Job.30.31">ver. 28-31</reference>. III. He had long enjoyed a good state of health, but now he was sick and in pain, <reference osisRef="Job.30.17-Job.30.19">ver. 17-19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">30</reference>. IV. Time was when the secret of God was with him, but now his communication with heaven was cut off, <reference osisRef="Job.30.20-Job.30.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. V. He had promised himself a long life, but now he saw death at the door, <reference osisRef="Job.30.23">ver. 23</reference>. One thing he mentions, which aggravated his affliction, that it surprised him when he looked for peace. But two things gave him some relief:—1. That his troubles would not follow him to the grave, <reference osisRef="Job.30.24">ver. 24</reference>. 2. That his conscience witnessed for him that, in his prosperity, he had sympathized with those that were in misery, <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">ver. 25</reference>.
entries.506505709afb6015bfefd7727130480cf8da242a: <div eID="gen9970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9969" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Humbled Condition. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But now <hi type="italic">they that are</hi> younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock. <hi type="super">2</hi> Yea, whereto <hi type="italic">might</hi> the strength of their hands <hi type="italic">profit</hi> me, in whom old age was perished? <hi type="super">3</hi> For want and famine <hi type="italic">they were</hi> solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste. 4 Who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots <hi type="italic">for</hi> their meat. <hi type="super">5</hi> They were driven forth from among <hi type="italic">men,</hi> (they cried after them as <hi type="italic">after</hi> a thief;) <hi type="super">6</hi> To dwell in the clifts of the valleys, <hi type="italic">in</hi> caves of the earth, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the rocks. <hi type="super">7</hi> Among the bushes they brayed; under the nettles they were gathered together. 8 <hi type="italic">They were</hi> children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth. <hi type="super">9</hi> And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword. <hi type="super">10</hi> They abhor me, they flee far from me, and spare not to spit in my face. <hi type="super">11</hi> Because he hath loosed my cord, and afflicted me, they have also let loose the bridle before me. <hi type="super">12</hi> Upon <hi type="italic">my</hi> right <hi type="italic">hand</hi> rise the youth; they push away my feet, and they raise up against me the ways of their destruction. <hi type="super">13</hi> They mar my path, they set forward my calamity, they have no helper. <hi type="super">14</hi> They came <hi type="italic">upon me</hi> as a wide breaking in <hi type="italic">of waters:</hi> in the desolation they rolled themselves <hi type="italic">upon me.</hi> <div eID="gen9971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9972" type="x-p"/> Here Job makes a very large and sad complaint of the great disgrace he had fallen into, from the height of honour and reputation, which was exceedingly grievous and cutting to such an ingenuous spirit as Job's was. Two things he insists upon as greatly aggravating his affliction:— <div eID="gen9972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9973" type="x-p"/> I. The meanness of the persons that affronted him. As it added much to his honour, in the day of his prosperity, that princes and nobles showed him respect and paid a deference to him, so it added no less to his disgrace in his adversity that he was spurned by the footmen, and trampled upon by those that were not only every way his inferiors, but were the meanest and most contemptible of all mankind. None can be represented as more base than those are here represented who insulted Job, upon all accounts. 1. They were young, younger than he (<reference osisRef="Job.30.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">the youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.30.12">v. 12</reference>), who ought to have behaved themselves respectfully towards him for his age and gravity. Even the children, in their play, played upon him, as the children of Bethel upon the prophet, <hi type="italic">Go up, thou bald-head.</hi> Children soon learn to be scornful when they see their parents so. 2. They were of a mean extraction. Their fathers were so very despicable that such a man as Job would have disdained to take them into the lowest service about his house, as that of tending the sheep and attending the shepherds with the dogs of his flock, <reference osisRef="Job.30.1">v. 1</reference>. They were so shabby that they were not fit to be seen among his servants, so silly that they were not fit to be employed, and so false that they were not fit to be trusted in the meanest post. Job here speaks of what he might have done, not of what he did: he was not of such a spirit as to set any of the children of men with the dogs of his flock; he knew the dignity of human nature better than to do so. 3. They and their families were the unprofitable burdens of the earth, and good for nothing. Job himself, with all his prudence and patience, could make nothing of them, <reference osisRef="Job.30.2">v. 2</reference>. The young were not fit for labour, they were so lazy, and went about their work so awkwardly: <hi type="italic">Whereto might the strength of their hands profit me?</hi> The old were not to be advised with in the smallest matters, for in them was old age indeed, but their <hi type="italic">old age was perished,</hi> they were twice children. 4. They were extremely poor, <reference osisRef="Job.30.3">v. 3</reference>. They were ready to starve, for they would not dig, and to beg they were ashamed. Had they been brought to necessity by the providence of God, their neighbours would have sought them out as proper objects of charity and would have relieved them; but, being brought into straits by their own slothfulness and wastefulness, nobody was forward to relieve them. Hence they were forced to flee into the deserts both for shelter and sustenance, and were put to sorry shifts indeed, when they <hi type="italic">cut up mallows by the bushes,</hi> and were glad to eat them, for want of food that was fit for them, <reference osisRef="Job.30.4">v. 4</reference>. See what hunger will bring men to: one half of the world does not know how the other half lives; yet those that have abundance ought to think sometimes of those whose fare is very coarse and who are brought to a short allowance of that too. But we must own the righteousness of God, and not think it strange, if slothfulness clothe men with rags and the idle soul be made to suffer hunger. This beggarly world is full of the devil's poor. 5. They were very scandalous wicked people, not only the burdens, but the plagues, of the places where they lived, arrant scoundrels, the scum of the country: <hi type="italic">They were driven forth from among men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.5">v. 5</reference>. They were such lying, thieving, lurking, mischievous people, that the best service the magistrates could do was to rid the country of them, while the very mob cried after them as after a thief. <hi type="italic">Away with such fellows from the earth; it is not fit they should live.</hi> They were lazy and would not work, and therefore they were exclaimed against as thieves, and justly; for those that do not earn their own bread by honest labour do, in effect, steal the bread out of other people's mouths. An idle fellow is a public nuisance; but it is better to drive such into a workhouse than, as here, into a wilderness, which will punish them indeed, but never reform them. They were forced to dwell in <hi type="italic">caves of the earth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they brayed</hi> like asses <hi type="italic">among the bushes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.6-Job.30.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. See what is the lot of those that have the cry of the country, the cry of their own conscience, against them; they cannot but be in a continual terror and confusion. <hi type="italic">They groan among the trees</hi> (so Broughton) <hi type="italic">and smart among the nettles;</hi> they are stung and scratched there, where they hoped to be sheltered and protected. See what miseries wicked people bring themselves to in this world; yet this is nothing to what is in reserve for them in the other world. 8. They had nothing at all in them to recommend them to any man's esteem. They were a vile kind; yea, a kind without fame, people that nobody could give a good word to nor had a good wish for; they were banished from the earth as being <hi type="italic">viler than the earth.</hi> One would not think it possible that ever the human nature should sink so low, and degenerate so far, as it did in these people. When we thank God that we are men we have reason to thank him that we are not such men. But such as these were abusive to Job, (1.) In revenge, because when he was in prosperity and power, like a good magistrate, he put in execution the laws which were in force against vagabonds, and rogues, and sturdy beggars, which these base people now remembered against him. (2.) In triumph over him, because they thought he had now become like one of them. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10-Isa.14.11">Isa. xiv. 10, 11</reference>. The abjects, men of mean spirits, insult over the miserable, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Ps. xxxv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen9973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9974" type="x-p"/> II. The greatness of the affronts that were given him. It cannot be imagined how abusive they were. <div eID="gen9974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9975" type="x-p"/> 1. They made ballads on him, with which they made themselves and their companions merry (<reference osisRef="Job.30.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am their song and their byword.</hi> Those have a very base spirit that turn the calamities of their honest neighbours into a jest, and can sport themselves with their griefs. <div eID="gen9975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9976" type="x-p"/> 2. They shunned him as a loathsome spectacle, abhorred him, fled far from him, (<reference osisRef="Job.30.10">v. 10</reference>), as an ugly monster or as one infected. Those that were themselves driven out from among men would have had him driven out. For, <div eID="gen9976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9977" type="x-p"/> 3. They expressed the greatest scorn and indignation against him. They spat in his face, or were ready to do so; they tripped up his heels, pushed away his feet (<reference osisRef="Job.30.12">v. 12</reference>), kicked him, either in wrath, because they hated him, or in sport, to make themselves merry with him, as they did with their companions at foot-ball. The best of saints have sometimes received the worst of injuries and indignities from a spiteful, scornful, wicked world, and must not think it strange; our Master himself was thus abused. <div eID="gen9977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9978" type="x-p"/> 4. They were very malicious against him, and not only made a jest of him, but made a prey of him—not only affronted him, but set themselves to do him all the real mischief they could devise: <hi type="italic">They raise up against me the ways of their destruction;</hi> or (as some read it), <hi type="italic">They cast upon me the cause of their woe;</hi> that is, "They lay the blame of their being driven out upon me;" and it is common for criminals to hate the judges and laws by which they are punished. But under this pretence, (1.) They accused him falsely, and misrepresented his former conversation, which is here called <hi type="italic">marring his path.</hi> They reflected upon him as a tyrant and an oppressor because he had done justice upon them; and perhaps Job's friends grounded their uncharitable censures of him (<reference osisRef="Job.22.6-Job.22.10">ch. xxii. 6</reference>, &c.) upon the unjust and unreasonable clamours of these sorry people; and it was an instance of their great weakness and inconsideration, for who can be innocent if the accusations of such persons may be heeded? (2.) They not only triumphed in his calamity, but set it forward, and did all they could to add to his miseries and make them more grievous to him. It is a great sin to forward the calamity of any, especially of good people. In this <hi type="italic">they have no helper,</hi> nobody to set them on or to countenance them in it, nobody to bear them out or to protect them, but they do it of their own accord; they are fools in other things, but wise enough to do mischief, and need no help in inventing that. Some read it thus, <hi type="italic">They hold my heaviness a profit, though they be never the better.</hi> Wicked people, though they get nothing by the calamities of others, yet rejoice in them. <div eID="gen9978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9979" type="x-p"/> 5. Those that did him all this mischief were numerous, unanimous, and violent (<reference osisRef="Job.30.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They came upon me as a wide breaking in of waters,</hi> when the dam is broken; or, "They came as soldiers into a broad breach which they have made in the wall of a besieged city, pouring in upon me with the utmost fury;" and in this they took a pride and a pleasure: <hi type="italic">They rolled themselves in the desolation</hi> as a man rolls himself in a soft and easy bed, and they rolled themselves upon him with all the weight of their malice. <div eID="gen9979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9980" type="x-p"/> III. All this contempt put upon him was caused by the troubles he was in (<reference osisRef="Job.30.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because he has loosed my cord,</hi> has taken away the honour and power with which I was girded (<reference osisRef="Job.12.18">ch. xii. 18</reference>), has scattered what I had got together and untwisted all my affairs—because he has afflicted me, therefore <hi type="italic">they have let loose the bridle before me,</hi>" that is, "have given themselves a liberty to say and do what they please against me." Those that by Providence are stripped of their honour may expect to be loaded with contempt by inconsiderate ill-natured people. "Because he hath loosed <hi type="italic">his</hi> cord" (the original has that reading also), that is, "because he has taken off his bridle of restraint from off their malice, they cast away the bridle from me," that is, "they make no account of my authority, nor stand in any awe of me." It is owing to the hold God has of the consciences even of bad men, and the restraints he lays upon them, that we are not continually thus insulted and abused; and, if at any time we meet with such ill treatment, we must acknowledge the hand of God in taking off those restraints, as David did when Shimei cursed him: <hi type="italic">So let him curse, for the Lord hath bidden him.</hi> Now in all this, 1. We may see the uncertainty of worldly honour, and particularly of popular applause, how suddenly a man may fall from the height of dignity into the depth of disgrace. What little cause therefore have men to be ambitious or proud of that which may be so easily lost, and what little confidence is to be put in it! Those that to-day cry <hi type="italic">Hosannah</hi> may to-morrow cry <hi type="italic">Crucify.</hi> But there is an honour which comes from God, which if we secure, we shall find it not thus changeable and loseable. 2. We may see that it has often been the lot of very wise and good men to be trampled upon and abused. And, 3. That those who look only at the things that are seen despise those whom the world frowns upon, though they are ever so much the favourites of Heaven. Nothing is more grievous in poverty than that it renders men contemptible. <hi type="italic">Turba Remi sequitur fortunam, ut semper odit damnatos—The Roman populace, faithful to the turns of fortune, still persecute the fallen.</hi> 4. We may see in Job a type of Christ, who was thus made a <hi type="italic">reproach of men</hi> and <hi type="italic">despised of the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.6">Ps. xxii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 3</reference>), and who hid not his face from shame and spitting, but bore the indignity better than Job did.
entries.4c99d1907b627c1b3b6acafe9084cc66c5a08182: <div eID="gen9980" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job Complains of His Affliction. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9981" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Terrors are turned upon me: they pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud. <hi type="super">16</hi> And now my soul is poured out upon me; the days of affliction have taken hold upon me. <hi type="super">17</hi> My bones are pierced in me in the night season: and my sinews take no rest. <hi type="super">18</hi> By the great force <hi type="italic">of my disease</hi> is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat. <hi type="super">19</hi> He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes. <hi type="super">20</hi> I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me: I stand up, and thou regardest me <hi type="italic">not.</hi> <hi type="super">21</hi> Thou art become cruel to me: with thy strong hand thou opposest thyself against me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride <hi type="italic">upon it,</hi> and dissolvest my substance. <hi type="super">23</hi> For I know <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou wilt bring me <hi type="italic">to</hi> death, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> the house appointed for all living. 24 Howbeit he will not stretch out <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand to the grave, though they cry in his destruction. <hi type="super">25</hi> Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? was <hi type="italic">not</hi> my soul grieved for the poor? <hi type="super">26</hi> When I looked for good, then evil came <hi type="italic">unto me:</hi> and when I waited for light, there came darkness. <hi type="super">27</hi> My bowels boiled, and rested not: the days of affliction prevented me. <hi type="super">28</hi> I went mourning without the sun: I stood up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I cried in the congregation. <hi type="super">29</hi> I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls. <hi type="super">30</hi> My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat. <hi type="super">31</hi> My harp also is <hi type="italic">turned</hi> to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep. <div eID="gen9981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9982" type="x-p"/> In this second part of Job's complaint, which is very bitter, and has a great many sorrowful accents in it, we may observe a great deal that he complains of and some little that he comforts himself with. <div eID="gen9982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9983" type="x-p"/> I. Here is much that he complains of. <div eID="gen9983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9984" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, it was a day of great affliction and sorrow. (1.) Affliction seized him, and surprised him. It seized him (<reference osisRef="Job.30.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The days of affliction have taken hold upon me, have caught me</hi> (so some); <hi type="italic">they have arrested me,</hi> as the bailiff arrests the debtor, claps him on the back, and secures him. When trouble comes with commission it will take fast hold, and not lose its hold. It surprised him (<reference osisRef="Job.30.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The days of affliction prevented me,</hi>" that is, "they came upon me without giving me any previous warning. I did not expect them, nor make any provision for such an evil day." Observe, He reckons his affliction by days, which will soon be numbered and finished, and are nothing to the ages of eternity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2 Cor. iv. 17</reference>. (2.) He was in great sorrow by reason of it. His <hi type="italic">bowels boiled</hi> with grief, <hi type="italic">and rested not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.27">v. 27</reference>. The sense of his calamities was continually preying upon his spirits without any intermission. He <hi type="italic">went mourning</hi> from day to day, always sighing, always weeping; and such cloud was constantly upon his mind that he went, in effect, <hi type="italic">without the sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.28">v. 28</reference>. He had nothing that he could take any comfort in. He abandoned himself to perpetual sorrow, as one that, like Jacob, resolved to go to the grave mourning. He walked out of the sun (so some) in dark shady places, as melancholy people use to do. If he went into the congregation, to join with them in solemn worship, instead of standing up calmly to desire their prayers, he <hi type="italic">stood up and cried</hi> aloud, through pain of body, or anguish of mind, like one half distracted. If he appeared in public, to receive visits, when the fit came upon him he could not contain himself, nor preserve due decorum, but stood up and shrieked aloud. Thus he was <hi type="italic">a brother to dragons and owls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.30.29">v. 29</reference>), both in choosing solitude and retirement, as they do (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa. xxxiv. 13</reference>), and in making a fearful hideous noise as they do; his inconsiderate complaints were fitly compared to their inarticulate ones. <div eID="gen9984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9985" type="x-p"/> 2. The terror and trouble that seized his soul were the sorest part of his calamity, <reference osisRef="Job.30.15-Job.30.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. (1.) If he looked forward, he saw every thing frightful before him: if he endeavoured to shake off his terrors, they turned furiously upon him: if he endeavoured to escape from them, they pursued his soul as swiftly and violently as the wind. He complained, at first, of the <hi type="italic">terrors of God setting themselves in array against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">ch. vi. 4</reference>. And still, which way soever he looked, they turned upon him; which way soever he fled, they pursued him. <hi type="italic">My soul</hi> (Heb., <hi type="italic">my principal one, my princess</hi>); the soul is the principal part of the man; it is our glory; it is every way more excellent than the body, and therefore that which pursues the soul, and threatens that, should be most dreaded. (2.) If he looked back, he saw all the good he had formerly enjoyed removed from him, and nothing left him but the bitter remembrance of it: <hi type="italic">My welfare</hi> and prosperity <hi type="italic">pass away,</hi> as suddenly, swiftly, and irrecoverably, <hi type="italic">as a cloud.</hi> (3.) If he looked within, he found his spirit quite sunk and unable to bear his infirmity, not only wounded, but <hi type="italic">poured out upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.16">v. 16</reference>. He was not only weak as water, but, in his own apprehension, lost as water spilt upon the ground. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Ps. xxii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">My heart is melted like wax.</hi> <div eID="gen9985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9986" type="x-p"/> 3. His bodily diseases were very grievous; for, (1.) He was full of pain, piercing pain, pain that went to the bone, to all his bones, <reference osisRef="Job.30.17">v. 17</reference>. It was a <hi type="italic">sword in his bones,</hi> which <hi type="italic">pierced him in the night season,</hi> when he should have been refreshed with sleep. His nerves were affected with strong convulsions; his <hi type="italic">sinews took no rest.</hi> By reason of his pain, he could take no rest, but sleep departed from his eyes. <hi type="italic">His bones were burnt with heat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">v. 30</reference>. He was in a constant fever, which dried up the radical moisture and even consumed the marrow in his bones. See how frail our bodies are, which carry in themselves the seeds of our own disease and death. (2.) He was full of sores. Some that are pained in their bones, yet sleep in a whole skin, but, Satan's commission against Job extending both to his bone and to his flesh, he spared neither. His <hi type="italic">skin was black upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">v. 30</reference>. The blood settled, and the sores suppurated and by degrees scabbed over, which made his skin look black. Even his garment had its colour changed with the continual running of his boils, and the soft clothing he used to wear had now grown so stiff that all his garments were <hi type="italic">like his collar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.18">v. 18</reference>. It would be noisome to describe what a condition poor Job was in for want of clean linen and good attendance, and what filthy rags all his clothes were. Some think that, among other diseases, Job was ill of a quinsy or swelling in his throat, and that it was this which bound him about like a stiff collar. Thus was he <hi type="italic">cast into the mire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.30.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">compared to mire</hi> (so some); his body looked more like a heap of dirt than any thing else. Let none be proud of their clothing nor proud of their cleanness; they know not but some disease or other may <hi type="italic">change their garments,</hi> and even <hi type="italic">throw them into the mire,</hi> and make them noisome both to themselves and others. <hi type="italic">Instead of sweet smell, there shall be a stench,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.3.24">Isa. iii. 24</reference>. We are but dust and ashes at the best, and our bodies are vile bodies; but we are apt to forget it, till God, by some sore disease, makes us sensibly to feel and own what we are. "<hi type="italic">I have become already like</hi> that <hi type="italic">dust and ashes</hi> into which I must shortly be resolved: wherever I go I carry my grave about with me." <div eID="gen9986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9987" type="x-p"/> 4. That which afflicted him most of all was that God seemed to be his enemy and to fight against him. It was <hi type="italic">he</hi> that <hi type="italic">cast him into the mire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.30.19">v. 19</reference>), and seemed to trample on him when he had him there. This cut him to the heart more than any thing else, (1.) That God did not appear for him. He addressed himself to him, but gained no grant—appealed to him, but gained no sentence; he was very importunate in his applications, but in vain (<reference osisRef="Job.30.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I cry unto thee,</hi> as one in earnest, <hi type="italic">I stand up,</hi> and cry, as one waiting for an answer, but thou hearest not, <hi type="italic">thou regardest not,</hi> for any thing I can perceive." If our most fervent prayers bring not in speedy and sensible returns, we must not think it strange. Though the seed of Jacob did never seek in vain, yet they have often thought that they did and that God has not only been deaf, but angry, at the prayers of his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>. (2.) That God did appear against him. That which he here says of God is one of the worst words that ever Job spoke (<reference osisRef="Job.30.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast become cruel to me.</hi> Far be it from the God of mercy and grace that he should be cruel to any (his compassions fail not), but especially that he should be so to his own children. Job was unjust and ungrateful when he said so of him: but harbouring hard thoughts of God was the sin which did, at this time, most easily beset him. Here, [1.] He thought God fought against him and stirred up his whole strength to ruin him: <hi type="italic">With thy strong hand thou opposest thyself,</hi> or art an adversary against me. He had better thoughts of God (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">ch. xxiii. 6</reference>) when he concluded he would <hi type="italic">not plead against him with his great power.</hi> God has an absolute sovereignty and an irresistible strength, but he never uses either the one or the other for the crushing or oppressing of any. [2.] He thought he insulted over him (<reference osisRef="Job.30.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou lifted me up to the wind,</hi> as a feather or the chaff which the wind plays with; so unequal a match did Job think himself for Omnipotence, and so unable was he to help himself when he was made to ride, not in triumph, but in terror, upon the wings of the wind, and the judgments of God did even <hi type="italic">dissolve his substance,</hi> as a cloud is dissolved and dispersed by the wind. Man's substance, take him in his best estate, is nothing before the power of God; it is soon dissolved. <div eID="gen9987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9988" type="x-p"/> 5. He expected no other now than that God, by these troubles, would shortly make an end of him: "If I be made to ride upon the wind, I can count upon no other than to break my neck shortly;" and he speaks as if God had no other design upon him than that in all his dealings with him: "<hi type="italic">I know that thou wilt bring me,</hi> with so much the more terror, <hi type="italic">to death,</hi> though I might have been brought thither without all this ado, for it is <hi type="italic">the house appointed for all living,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.30.23">v. 23</reference>. The grave is a house, a narrow, dark, cold, ill-furnished house, but it will be our residence, where we shall rest and be safe. It is our long home, our own home; for it is our mother's lap, and in it we are gathered to our fathers. It is a house appointed for us by him that has appointed us the bounds of all our habitations. It is appointed for all the living. It is the common receptacle, where rich and poor meet; it is appointed for the general rendezvous. We must all be brought thither shortly. It is God that brings us to it, for the keys of death and the grave are in his hand, and we may all know that, sooner or later, he will bring us thither. It would be well for us if we would duly consider it. <hi type="italic">The living know that they shall die;</hi> let us, each of us, know it with application. <div eID="gen9988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9989" type="x-p"/> 6. There were two things that aggravated his trouble, and made it the less tolerable:—(1.) That it was a very great disappointment to his expectation (<reference osisRef="Job.30.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When I looked for good,</hi> for more good, or at least for the continuance of what I had, <hi type="italic">then evil came</hi>"—such uncertain things are all our worldly enjoyments, and such a folly is it to feed ourselves with great expectations from them. Those that wait for light from the sparks of their creature comforts will be wretchedly disappointed and will <hi type="italic">make their bed in the darkness.</hi> (2.) That is was a very great change in his condition (<reference osisRef="Job.30.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My harp is</hi> not only laid by, and hung upon the willow-trees, but it is <hi type="italic">turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those that weep.</hi>" Job, in his prosperity, had taken <hi type="italic">the timbrel and harp,</hi> and <hi type="italic">rejoiced at the sound of the organ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.12">ch. xxi. 12</reference>. Notwithstanding his gravity and grace, he had found time to be cheerful; but now his tune was altered. Let those therefore that rejoice be <hi type="italic">as though they rejoiced not,</hi> for they know not how soon their <hi type="italic">laughter</hi> will be <hi type="italic">turned into mourning and their joy into heaviness.</hi> Thus we see how much Job complains of; but, <div eID="gen9989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9990" type="x-p"/> II. Here is something in the midst of all with which he comforts himself, and it is but a little. 1. He foresees, with comfort, that death will be the period of all his calamities (<reference osisRef="Job.30.24">v. 24</reference>): Though God now, with a strong hand, opposed himself against him, "yet," says he, "<hi type="italic">he will not stretch out his hand to the grave.</hi>" The hand of God's wrath would bring him to death, but would not follow him beyond death; his soul would be safe and happy in the world of spirits, his body safe and easy in the dust. Though men <hi type="italic">cry in his destruction</hi> (though, when they are dying, there is a great deal of agony and out-cry, many a sigh, and groan, and complaint), yet in the grave they feel nothing, they fear nothing, but all is quiet there. "Though in hell, which is called <hi type="italic">destruction,</hi> they cry, yet not in the grave; and, being delivered from the second death, the first to me will be an effectual relief." Therefore he wished he might be <hi type="italic">hidden in the grave,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">ch. xiv. 13</reference>. 2. He reflects with comfort upon the concern he always had for the calamities of others when he was himself at ease (<reference osisRef="Job.30.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?</hi> Some think he herein complains of God, thinking it very hard that he who had shown mercy to others should not himself find mercy. I would rather take it as a quieting consideration to himself; his conscience witnessed for him that he had always sympathized with persons in misery and done what he could to help them, and therefore he had reason to expect that, at length, both God and his friends would pity him. Those who mourn with them that mourn will bear their own sorrows the better when it comes to their turn to drink of the bitter cup. <hi type="italic">Did not my soul burn for the poor?</hi> so some read it, comparing it with that of St. Paul, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.29">2 Cor. xi. 29</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who is offended, and I burn not?</hi> As those who have been unmerciful and hard-hearted to others may expect to hear of it from their own consciences, when they are themselves in trouble, so those who have considered the poor and succoured them shall have the remembrance thereof to make their bed easy in their sickness, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Ps. xli. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.3">3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Job.30"/> <div eID="gen9990" type="x-p"/>

entries.3f06ebbaac48be2a82435e8c26d3693a1d48966c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5092"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 30</title> <div sID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.31">Job 30:1-31</reference>.<div eID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5092"/><hi type="bold">1. younger--</hi>not the three friends (<reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.32.4">32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.7">6, 7</reference>). A general description: <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.8">Job 30:1-8</reference>, the lowness of the persons who derided him; <reference osisRef="Job.30.9-Job.30.15">Job 30:9-15</reference>, the derision itself. Formerly old men rose to me (<reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>). Now not only my juniors, who are bound to reverence me (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Le 19:32</reference>), but even the mean and base-born actually deride me; opposed to, "smiled upon" (<reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference>). This goes farther than even the "mockery" of Job by relations and friends (<reference osisRef="Job.12.4">Job 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.16.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.22">19:22</reference>). Orientals feel keenly any indignity shown by the young. Job speaks as a rich Arabian emir, proud of his descent.<div eID="gen7556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dogs--</hi>regarded with disgust in the East as unclean (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">1Sa 17:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pr 26:11</reference>). They are not allowed to enter a house, but run about wild in the open air, living on offal and chance morsels (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.14">Psa 59:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">15</reference>). Here again we are reminded of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>). "Their fathers, my coevals, were so mean and famished that I would not have associated them with (not to say, set them over) my dogs in guarding my flock." <div eID="gen7557" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a4bfb2b7947fba59ef88a7df29e36a6aa1d1718: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5093"/><div sID="gen7558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5093"/>2. If their fathers could be of no profit to me, much less the sons, who are feebler than their sires; and in whose case the hope of attaining old age is utterly gone, so puny are they (<reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>) [Maurer]. Even if they had "strength of hands," that could be now of no use to me, as all I want in my present affliction is sympathy. <div eID="gen7558" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6b003dbef4eae1e5add5684d5a12601b73efe23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5094"/><div sID="gen7559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5094"/><hi type="bold">3. solitary--</hi>literally, "hard as a rock"; so translate, rather, "dried up," emaciated with hunger. Job describes the rudest race of Bedouins of the desert [Umbreit].<div eID="gen7559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fleeing--</hi>So the Septuagint. Better, as Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate, "gnawers of the wilderness." What they gnaw follows in <reference osisRef="Job.30.4">Job 30:4</reference>.<div eID="gen7560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in former time--</hi>literally, the "yesternight of desolation and waste" (the most utter desolation; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference>); that is, those deserts frightful as night to man, and even there from time immemorial. I think both ideas are in the words darkness [Gesenius] and antiquity [Umbreit]. (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen7561" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4f049152413117c06ed2291ec7648c75d143c21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5095"/><div sID="gen7562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5095"/><hi type="bold">4. mallows--</hi>rather, "salt-wort," which grows in deserts and is eaten as a salad by the poor [Maurer].<div eID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the bushes--</hi>among the bushes.<div eID="gen7563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">juniper--</hi>rather, a kind of broom, Spartium junceum [Linnæus], still called in Arabia, as in the Hebrew of Job, retem, of which the bitter roots are eaten by the poor. <div eID="gen7564" type="x-p"/>
entries.48606ad5389b3820c511dad3cdf22d0b7c7412d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5096"/><div sID="gen7565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5096"/><hi type="bold">5. they cried--</hi>that is, "a cry is raised." Expressing the contempt felt for this race by civilized and well-born Arabs. When these wild vagabonds make an incursion on villages, they are driven away, as thieves would be. <div eID="gen7565" type="x-p"/>
entries.8236be0f7bb539748f56ea0a3715b0224c162390: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5097"/><div sID="gen7566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5097"/>6. They are forced "to dwell."<div eID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cliffs of the valleys--</hi>rather, "in the gloomy valleys"; literally, "in the gloom of the valleys," or wadies. To dwell in valleys is, in the East, a mark of wretchedness. The troglodytes, in parts of Arabia, lived in such dwellings as caves. <div eID="gen7567" type="x-p"/>
entries.1de54a185467ee13f73dfe82d407a4bf679945bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5098"/><div sID="gen7568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5098"/><hi type="bold">7. brayed--</hi>like the wild ass (<reference osisRef="Job.6.5">Job 6:5</reference> for food). The inarticulate tones of this uncivilized rabble are but little above those of the beast of the field.<div eID="gen7568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gathered together--</hi>rather, sprinkled here and there. Literally, "poured out," graphically picturing their disorderly mode of encampment, lying up and down behind the thorn bushes.<div eID="gen7569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nettles--</hi>or brambles [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7570" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cf09ebd6802ee5ee21725c118f1cad15d29f47e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5099"/><div sID="gen7571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5099"/><hi type="bold">8. fools--</hi>that is, the impious and abandoned (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.25">1Sa 25:25</reference>).<div eID="gen7571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">base--</hi>nameless, low-born rabble.<div eID="gen7572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">viler than, &c.--</hi>rather, they were driven or beaten out of the land. The Horites in Mount Seir (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">Ge 14:6</reference> with which compare <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20">Ge 36:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.12">De 2:12</reference>, 22) were probably the aborigines, driven out by the tribe to which Job's ancestors belonged; their name means troglodytæ, or "dwellers in caves." To these Job alludes here (<reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.8">Job 30:1-8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.24.4-Gen.24.8">Ge 24:4-8</reference>, which compare together). <div eID="gen7573" type="x-p"/>
entries.93abfb4d1612440f1f18b729a1897a9019d07aee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5100"/><div sID="gen7574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5100"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job 17:6</reference>). Strikingly similar to the derision Jesus Christ underwent (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">La 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.12">Psa 69:12</reference>). Here Job returns to the sentiment in <reference osisRef="Job.30.1">Job 30:1</reference>. It is to such I am become a song of "derision." <div eID="gen7574" type="x-p"/>
entries.3517aee5fd142ca619e37fa52bdcb03e8e7263c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5101"/><div sID="gen7575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5101"/><hi type="bold">10. in my face--</hi>rather, refrain not to spit in deliberate contempt before my face. To spit at all in presence of another is thought in the East insulting, much more so when done to mark "abhorrence." Compare the further insult to Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.67">Mt 26:67</reference>). <div eID="gen7575" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a3c27b6d6c459aeee9c7ce446ef1cb8a37916ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5102"/><div sID="gen7576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5102"/><hi type="bold">11. He--</hi>that is, "God"; antithetical to "they"; English Version here follows the marginal reading (Keri).<div eID="gen7576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my cord--</hi>image from a bow unstrung; opposed to <reference osisRef="Job.29.20">Job 29:20</reference>. The text (Chetib), "His cord" or "reins" is better; "yea, each lets loose his reins" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7577" type="x-p"/>
entries.51bc4ca5b78288633ec0230b8810c311e614b678: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5103"/><div sID="gen7578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5103"/><hi type="bold">12. youth--</hi>rather, a (low) brood. To rise on the right hand is to accuse, as that was the position of the accuser in court (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>).<div eID="gen7578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">push ... feet--</hi>jostle me out of the way (<reference osisRef="Job.24.4">Job 24:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ways of--</hi>that is, their ways of (that is, with a view to my) destruction. Image, as in <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference>, from a besieging army throwing up a way of approach for itself to a city. <div eID="gen7580" type="x-p"/>
entries.94f6df958e9242e2678af497c7c48efbc3e029b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5104"/><div sID="gen7581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5104"/>13. Image of an assailed fortress continued. They tear up the path by which succor might reach me.<div eID="gen7581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set forward--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zec 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they have no helper--</hi>Arabic proverb for contemptible persons. Yet even such afflict Job. <div eID="gen7583" type="x-p"/>
entries.69079c0cc157463579481d18cd83037c61f8474b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5105"/><div sID="gen7584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5105"/><hi type="bold">14. waters--</hi>(So <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.20">2Sa 5:20</reference>). But it is better to retain the image of <reference osisRef="Job.30.12">Job 30:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.30.13">13</reference>. "They came [upon me] as through a wide breach," namely, made by the besiegers in the wall of a fortress (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.13">Is 30:13</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen7584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the desolation--</hi>"Amidst the crash" of falling masonry, or "with a shout like the crash" of, &c. <div eID="gen7585" type="x-p"/>
entries.6802381ebe671332443f33731f795ecea437359f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5106"/><div sID="gen7586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5106"/><hi type="bold">15. they--</hi>terrors.<div eID="gen7586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soul--</hi>rather, "my dignity" [Umbreit].<div eID="gen7587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">welfare--</hi>prosperity.<div eID="gen7588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cloud--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.7.9">Job 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">Is 44:22</reference>). <div eID="gen7589" type="x-p"/>
entries.1cd1230e2aa3f0c39cde781973033e88136b0e6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5107"/><div sID="gen7590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5107"/>16-23. Job's outward calamities affect his mind.<div eID="gen7590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poured out--</hi>in irrepressible complaints (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.5">Jos 7:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7591" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eb14641edfaf3c4131472f024d28b7402318ec7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5114"/><div sID="gen7603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5114"/><hi type="bold">24. Expressing Job's faith as to the state after death. Though one must go to the grave, yet He will no more afflict in the ruin of the body (so Hebrew for "grave") there, if one has cried to Him when being destroyed. The "stretching of His hand" to punish after death answers antithetically to the raising "the cry" of prayer in the second clause. Maurer gives another translation which accords with the scope of <reference osisRef="Job.30.24-Job.30.31">Job 30:24-31</reference>; if it be natural for one in affliction to ask aid, why should it be considered (by the friends) wrong in my case? "Nevertheless does not a man in ruin stretch out his hand" (imploring help, <reference osisRef="Job.30.20">Job 30:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.17">La 1:17</reference>)? If one be in his calamity (destruction) is there not therefore a "cry" (for aid)? Thus in the parallelism "cry" answers to "stretch--</hi>hand"; "in his calamity," to "in ruin." The negative of the first clause is to be supplied in the second, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job 30:25</reference> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7603" type="x-p"/>
entries.73cee66e4b1094e0fb9d729349f6dfdb21d37b5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5115"/><div sID="gen7604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5115"/>25. May I not be allowed to complain of my calamity, and beg relief, seeing that I myself sympathized with those "in trouble" (literally, "hard of day"; those who had a hard time of it). <div eID="gen7604" type="x-p"/>
entries.91654f6776023b190a652929e06a8702e1a8505b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5116"/><div sID="gen7605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5116"/>26. I may be allowed to crave help, seeing that, "when I looked for good (on account of my piety and charity), yet evil," &c.<div eID="gen7605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.22.28">Job 22:28</reference>). <div eID="gen7606" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cb4830ca7b773a85bb681589773abd4ada5da69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5117"/><div sID="gen7607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5117"/><hi type="bold">27. bowels--</hi>regarded as the seat of deep feeling (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Is 16:11</reference>).<div eID="gen7607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boiled--</hi>violently heated and agitated.<div eID="gen7608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prevented--</hi>Old English for "unexpectedly came upon" me, "surprised" me. <div eID="gen7609" type="x-p"/>
entries.345c68a645148957029aacf5ba08f2da6c0876b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5118"/><div sID="gen7610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5118"/><hi type="bold">28. mourning--</hi>rather, I move about blackened, though not by the sun; that is, whereas many are blackened by the sun, I am, by the heat of God's wrath (so "boiled," <reference osisRef="Job.30.27">Job 30:27</reference>); the elephantiasis covering me with blackness of skin (<reference osisRef="Job.30.30">Job 30:30</reference>), as with the garb of mourning (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jr 14:2</reference>). This striking enigmatic form of Hebrew expression occurs, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Is 29:9</reference>.<div eID="gen7610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood up--</hi>as an innocent man crying for justice in an assembled court (<reference osisRef="Job.30.20">Job 30:20</reference>). <div eID="gen7611" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d2984a6fd2b6f7b2b8ca1bc54e53bcb26f76c27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5119"/><div sID="gen7612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5119"/><hi type="bold">29. dragons ... owls--</hi>rather, "jackals," "ostriches," both of which utter dismal screams (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mi 1:8</reference>); in which respect, as also in their living amidst solitudes (the emblem of desolation), Job is their brother and companion; that is, resembles them. "Dragon," Hebrew, tannim, usually means the crocodile; so perhaps here, its open jaws lifted towards heaven, and its noise making it seem as if it mourned over its fate [Bochart]. <div eID="gen7612" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e6d7496301b6d6591e0cd0002cc313461db3278: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5120"/><div sID="gen7613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5120"/><hi type="bold">30. upon me--</hi>rather, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.17">Job 30:17</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Job.30.17">Job 30:17</reference>), "my skin is black (and falls away) from me."<div eID="gen7613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my bones--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7614" type="x-p"/>
entries.04638ec816ce55fe313076dfb5b18ec18480aed1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5121"/><div sID="gen7615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5121"/><hi type="bold">31. organ--</hi>rather, "pipe" (<reference osisRef="Job.21.12">Job 21:12</reference>). "My joy is turned into the voice of weeping" (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.15">La 5:15</reference>). These instruments are properly appropriated to joy (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Is 30:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">32</reference>), which makes their use now in sorrow the sadder by contrast. <chapter eID="Job.30"/>

entries.0dd3ee31eb0618b75c03c3963ae5b8278f4673a8: <div eID="gen17343" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17344" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17345" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17345" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17344" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17346" type="x-p"/> Job proceeds to lament the change of his former condition, and the contempt into which his adversity had brought him, <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.15">Job 30:1-15</reference>. Pathetically describes the afflictions of his body and mind, vv. 16-31. <div eID="gen17346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17348" type="x-p"/> But now they that are younger than I have me in derision - Compare this with <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>, where he speaks of the respect he had from the youth while in the days of his prosperity. Now he is no longer affluent, and they are no longer respectful. <div eID="gen17348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17349" type="x-p"/> Dogs of my flock - Persons who were not deemed sufficiently respectable to be trusted with the care of those dogs which were the guardians of my flocks. Not confidential enough to be made shepherds, ass-keepers, or camel-drivers; nor even to have the care of the dogs by which the flocks were guarded. This saying is what we call an expression of sovereign contempt.
entries.49464a6b9ffd47f8e9b8d9c7b6dc3b0455e65aef: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17350" type="x-p"/> The strength of their hands profit me - He is speaking here of the fathers of these young men. What was the strength of their hands to me? Their old age also has perished. The sense of which I believe to be this: I have never esteemed their strength even in their most vigorous youth, nor their conduct, nor their counsel even in old age. They were never good for any thing, either young or old. As their youth was without profit, so their old age was without honor. See Calmet. Mr. Good contends that the words are Arabic, and should be translated according to the meaning in that language, and the first clause of the third verse joined to the latter clause of the second, without which no good meaning can be elicited so as to keep properly close to the letter. I shall give the Hebrew text, Mr. Good's Arabic, and its translation: - <div eID="gen17350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17351" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew text is this: - עלימו אבד כלח aleymo abad calach בחסר ובכפן גלמוד becheser ubechaphan galmud. <div eID="gen17351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17352" type="x-p"/> The Arabic version which he translates thus: - "With whom crabbed looks are perpetual, <div eID="gen17352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17353" type="x-p"/> From hunger and flinty famine." <div eID="gen17353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17354" type="x-p"/> This translation is very little distant from the import of the present Hebrew text, if it may be called Hebrew, when the principal words are pure Arabic, and the others constructively so.
entries.a3f87fd0245edbf786741b091e7ddb03c842d598: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17355" type="x-p"/> Fleeing into the wilderness - Seeking something to sustain life even in the barren desert. This shows the extreme of want, when the desert is supposed to be the only place where any thing to sustain life can possibly be found.
entries.58ed2bb97c2a0902ffc4ca580551c6bdc4f2b8f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17356" type="x-p"/> Who cut up mallows by the bushes - מלוח malluach, which we translate mallows, comes from מלח melach, salt; some herb or shrub of a salt nature, sea-purslane, or the salsaria, salsola, or saltwort. Bochart says it is the ἁλιμος of the Greeks, and the halimus of the Romans. Some translate it nettles. The Syriac and Arabic omit the whole verse. The halimus, or atriplex halimus, grows near the sea in different countries, and is found in Spain, America, England, and Barbary. The salsaria, salsola, or saltwort, is an extensive genus of plants, several common to Asia, and not a few indigenous to a dry and sandy soil. <div eID="gen17356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17357" type="x-p"/> And juniper roots for their meat - רתמים rethamim. This is variously translated juniper, broom, furze, gorse, or whin. It is supposed to derive its name from the toughness of its twigs, as רתם ratham signifies to bind; and this answers well enough to the broom. Genista quoque vinculi usum praestat, "The broom serves for bands," says Pliny, Hist. Nat. lib. xxiv., c. 9. But how can it be said that the roots of this shrub were eaten? I do not find any evidence from Asiatic writers that the roots of the juniper tree were an article of food; and some have supposed, because of this want of evidence, that the word לחמם lachmam, for their bread, should be understood thus, to bake their bread, because it is well known that the wood of the juniper gives an intense heat, and the coals of it endure a long time; and therefore we find coals of juniper, גחלי רחמים gachaley rethamim, used <reference osisRef="Psa.120.4">Psa 120:4</reference> to express severe and enduring punishment. But that the roots of the juniper were used for food in the northern countries, among the Goths, we have a positive testimony from Olaus Magnus, himself a Goth, and archbishop of Upsal, in lib. vii., c. 4, of his Hist. de Gentibus Septentrionalibus. Speaking of the great number of different trees in their woods, he says: "There is a great plenty of beech trees in all the northern parts, the virtue whereof is this: that, being cut between the bark and the wood, they send forth a juice that is good for drink. The fruit of them in famine serves for bread, and their bark for clothing. Likewise also the berries of the juniper, yea, even the roots of this tree are eaten for bread, as holy Job testifies, though it is difficult to come at them by reason of their prickles: in these prickles, or thorns, live coals will last a whole year. If the inhabitants do not quench them, when winds arise they set the woods on fire, and destroy all the circumjacent fields." In this account both the properties of the juniper tree, referred to by Job and David, are mentioned by the Gothic prelate. They use its berries and roots for food, and its wood for fire.
entries.85ef4f7c7013a83ba083002ef262bb287500b411: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17358" type="x-p"/> They were driven forth - They were persons whom no one would employ; they were driven away from the city; and if any of them appeared, the hue and cry was immediately raised up against them. The last clause Mr. Good translates, "They slunk away from them like a thief," instead of "They cried after them," etc.
entries.1eb10fde587b899445a372734389b62c0f575f19: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17359" type="x-p"/> To dwell in the cliffs of the valleys - They were obliged to take shelter in the most dangerous, out-of-the-way, and unfrequented places. This is the meaning.
entries.2e535b3c5e3e5c8109d05f98d01b0fdf200b7376: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17360" type="x-p"/> Among the bushes they brayed - They cried out among the bushes, seeking for food, as the wild ass when he is in want of provender. Two MSS. read ינאקו yinaku, they groaned, instead of ינהקו yinhaku, they brayed. <div eID="gen17360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17361" type="x-p"/> Under the nettles - חרול charul, the briers or brambles, under the brushwood in the thickest parts of the underwood; they huddled together like wild beasts.
entries.591a430a50b2f87ffb8f52367fb197d3f60673b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17362" type="x-p"/> Children of fools - Children of nabal; children without a name; persons of no consideration, and descendants of such. <div eID="gen17362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17363" type="x-p"/> Viler than the earth - Rather, driven out of the land; persons not fit for civil society.
entries.bf8f006102516c4a55d05e758d07b80e477f9521: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17364" type="x-p"/> Now am I their song - I am the subject of their mirth, and serve as a proverb or by-word. They use me with every species of indignity.
entries.1251f6fea73993c046e2ffdb9185bec191f2e08e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17365" type="x-p"/> They abhor me - What a state must civil society be in when such indignities were permitted to be offered to the aged and afflicted!
entries.941a33e6559d062015092c09ef411c7b0e535184: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17366" type="x-p"/> Because he hath loosed my cord - Instead of יתרי yithri, my cord, which is the keri or marginal reading, יתרו yithro, his cord, is the reading of the text in many copies; and this reading directs us to a metaphor taken from an archer, who, observing his butt, sets his arrow on the string, draws it to a proper degree of tension, levels, and then loosing his hold, the arrow flies at the mark. He hath let loose his arrow against me; it has hit me; and I am wounded. The Vulgate understood it in this way: Pharetram enim suam aperuit. So also the Septuagint: Ανοιξας γαρ φαρετραν αυτου; "He hath opened his quiver." <div eID="gen17366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17367" type="x-p"/> They have also let loose the bridle - When they perceived that God had afflicted me, they then threw off all restraints; like headstrong horses, swallowed the bit, got the reins on their own neck, and ran off at full speed.
entries.32de0ce37ac2ab9a7592341c1eebb72c362c9ecf: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17368" type="x-p"/> Upon my right hand rise the youth - The word פרחח pirchach, which we translate youth, signifies properly buds, or the buttons of trees. Mr. Good has younglings. Younkers would be better, were it not too colloquial. <div eID="gen17368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17369" type="x-p"/> They push away my feet - They trip up my heels, or they in effect trample me under their feet. They rush upon and overwhelm me. They are violently incensed against me. They roll themselves upon me, התגלגלו hithgalgalu, velut unda impellit undam, as waves of the sea which wash the sand from under the feet, and then swamp the man to the bottom; see <reference osisRef="Job.30.14">Job 30:14</reference>.
entries.ec54eeec7812e39db75062046d58591f7d8bf590: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17370" type="x-p"/> They mar my path - They destroy the way-marks, so that there is no safety in travelling through the deserts, the guide-posts and way-marks being gone. These may be an allusion here to a besieged city: the besiegers strive by every means and way to distress the besieged; stopping up the fountains, breaking up the road, raising up towers to project arrows and stones into the city, called here raising up against it the ways of destruction, <reference osisRef="Job.30.12">Job 30:12</reference>; preventing all succor and support. <div eID="gen17370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17371" type="x-p"/> They have no helper - "There is not an adviser among them." - Mr. Good. There is none to give them better instruction.
entries.da46496324c53641f8fcdda0f600db183994b05c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17372" type="x-p"/> They came upon me as a wide breaking in - They storm me on every side. <div eID="gen17372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17373" type="x-p"/> In the desolation they rolled themselves - When they had made the breach, they rolled in upon me as an irresistible torrent. There still appears to be an allusion to a besieged city: the sap, the breach, the storm, the flight, the pursuit, and the slaughter. See the following verse, <reference osisRef="Job.30.15">Job 30:15</reference> (note).
entries.40df55f3081db4e7ec0bc21820db7c8e39013999: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17374" type="x-p"/> Terrors are turned upon me - Defence is no longer useful; they have beat down my walls. <div eID="gen17374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17375" type="x-p"/> They pursue my soul as the wind - I seek safety in flight, my strong holds being no longer tenable; but they pursue me so swiftly, that it is impossible for me to escape. They follow me like a whirlwind; and as fast as that drives away the clouds before it, so is my prosperity destroyed. The word נדבתי nedibathi, which we translate my soul, signifies properly my nobility, my excellence: they endeavor to destroy both my reputation and my property.
entries.12154da2a934a11a6e23c6bcb971fb06f6a72e80: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17376" type="x-p"/> Is my garment changed - There seem to be here plain allusions to the effect of his cruel disease; the whole body being enveloped with a kind of elephantine hide, formed by innumerable incrustations from the ulcerated surface. <div eID="gen17376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17377" type="x-p"/> It bindeth me about - There is now a new kind of covering to my body, formed by the effects of this disease; and it is not a garment which I can cast off; it is as closely attached to me as the collar of my coat. Or, my disease seizes me as a strong armed man; it has throttled me, and cast me in the mud. This is probably an allusion to two persons struggling: the stronger seizes the other by the throat, brings him down, and treads him in the dirt.
entries.541616000821e196c22beead7c08e6d3d437257b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17378" type="x-p"/> I cry unto thee - I am persecuted by man, afflicted with sore disease, and apparently forsaken of God. <div eID="gen17378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17379" type="x-p"/> I stand up - Or, as some translate, "I persevere, and thou lookest upon me." Thou seest my desolate, afflicted state; but thine eye doth not affect thy heart. Thou leavest me unsupported to struggle with my adversities.
entries.28e5dfc649cf88c1b481c68955b2edc7543931b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17380" type="x-p"/> Thou art become cruel to me - Thou appearest to treat me with cruelty. I cry for mercy, trust in thy goodness, and am still permitted to remain under my afflictions. <div eID="gen17380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17381" type="x-p"/> Thou opposest thyself - Instead of helping, thou opposest me; thou appearest as my enemy.
entries.bb77217d6ccf860a50b62f1c694158a7a7026ff1: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17382" type="x-p"/> Thou liftest me up to the wind - Thou hast so completely stripped me of all my substance, that I am like chaff lifted up by the wind; or as a straw, the sport of every breeze; and at last carried totally away, being dissipated into particles by the continued agitation.
entries.64c6e4cef0fbc5aacb5f41be92d4fd846c804b89: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17383" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt bring me to death - This must be the issue of my present affliction: to God alone it is possible that I should survive it. <div eID="gen17383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17384" type="x-p"/> To the house appointed for all living - Or to the house, מועד moed, the rendezvous, the place of general assembly of human beings: the great devourer in whose jaws all that have lived, now live, and shall live, must necessarily meet. " - O great man-eater! <div eID="gen17384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17385" type="x-p"/> Whose every day is carnival; not sated yet! <div eID="gen17385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17386" type="x-p"/> Unheard of epicure! without a fellow! <div eID="gen17386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17387" type="x-p"/> The veriest gluttons do not always cram! <div eID="gen17387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17388" type="x-p"/> Some intervals of abstinence are sought <div eID="gen17388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17389" type="x-p"/> To edge the appetite: thou seekest none. <div eID="gen17389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17390" type="x-p"/> Methinks the countless swarms thou hast devour'd, <div eID="gen17390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17391" type="x-p"/> And thousands that each hour thou gobblest up, <div eID="gen17391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17392" type="x-p"/> This, less than this, might gorge thee to the full. <div eID="gen17392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17393" type="x-p"/> But O! rapacious still, thou gap'st for more, <div eID="gen17393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17394" type="x-p"/> Like one, whole days defrauded of his meals, <div eID="gen17394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17395" type="x-p"/> On whom lank hunger lays her skinny hand, <div eID="gen17395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17396" type="x-p"/> And whets to keenest eagerness his cravings; <div eID="gen17396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17397" type="x-p"/> As if diseases, massacres, and poisons, <div eID="gen17397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17398" type="x-p"/> Famine, and war, were not thy caterers." <div eID="gen17398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17399" type="x-p"/> The Grave.
entries.245ba68a665026d762332d232e231fa0baa40685: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17400" type="x-p"/> He will not stretch out his hand to the grave - After all that has been said relative to the just translation and true meaning of this verse, is it not evident that it is in the mouth of Job a consolatory reflection? As if he said, Though I suffer here, I shall not suffer hereafter. Though he add stroke to stroke, so as to destroy my life, yet his displeasure shall not proceed beyond the grave. <div eID="gen17400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17401" type="x-p"/> Though they cry in his destruction - Mr. Good translates: Surely there, in its ruin, is freedom. In the sepulcher there is freedom from calamity, and rest for the weary.
entries.3d6e34a5ba919bf10d9f3313bdc27a69673f0b37: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen17401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17402" type="x-p"/> Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? - Mr. Good translates much nearer the sense of the original, לקשה יום liksheh yom. "Should I not then weep for the ruthless day?" May I not lament that my sufferings are only to terminate with my life? Or, Did I not mourn for those who suffered by times of calamity? Was not my soul grieved for the poor? Did I not relieve the distressed according to my power; and did I not sympathize with the sufferer?
entries.84a8361f4ee5fa8aa59dd02b229a03e93a749f6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen17402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17403" type="x-p"/> My bowels boiled - This alludes to the strong commotion in the bowels which every humane person feels at the sight of one in misery.
entries.4f52849b060076cd284c5f5f39e886feadbdb472: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen17403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17404" type="x-p"/> I went mourning without the sun - חמה chammah, which we here translate the sun, comes from a root of the same letters, which signifies to hide, protect, etc., and may be translated, I went mourning without a protector or guardian; or, the word may be derived from חם cham, to be hot, and here it may signify fury, rage, anger; and thus it was understood by the Vulgate: Maerens incedebam, sine furore, I went mourning without anger; or, as Calmet translates, Je marchois tout triste, mais sans me laisser aller a l'emportement; "I walked in deep sadness, but did not give way to an angry spirit." The Syriac and Arabic understood it in the same way.
entries.0dd9b42546e5593352c94ed5844d1c31d8a315b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen17404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17405" type="x-p"/> I am a brother to dragons - By my mournful and continual cry I resemble תנים tannim, the jackals or hyenas. <div eID="gen17405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17406" type="x-p"/> And a companion to owls - בנות יענה benoth yaanah, to the daughters of howling: generally understood to be the ostrich; for both the jackal and the female ostrich are remarkable for their mournful cry, and for their attachment to desolate places - Dodd.
entries.0062068b5063a2d35e2a6e961199af59ba9804a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen17406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17407" type="x-p"/> My skin is black - By continual exposure to the open air, and parching influence of the sun. <div eID="gen17407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17408" type="x-p"/> My bones are burned with heat - A strong expression, to point out the raging fever that was continually preying upon his vitals.
entries.a4f1b63a465102443fbf36a206e11270e97c567b: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen17408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17409" type="x-p"/> My harp also is turned to mourning - Instead of the harp, my only music is my own plaintive cries. <div eID="gen17409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17410" type="x-p"/> And my organ - What the עגב uggab was, we know not; it was most probably some sort of pipe or wind instrument. His harp, כנור kinnor, and his pipe, עגב uggab, were equally mute, or only used for mournful ditties. <div eID="gen17410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17411" type="x-p"/> This chapter is full of the most painful and pathetic sorrow; but nevertheless tempered with a calmness and humiliation of spirit, which did not appear in Job's lamentations previously to the time in which he had that remarkable revelation mentioned in the nineteenth chapter. (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>) After he was assured that his Redeemer was the living God, he submitted to his dispensations, kissed the rod, and mourned not without hope, though in deep distress, occasioned by his unremitting sufferings. If the groaning of Job was great, his stroke was certainly heavy.  <chapter eID="Job.30"/> <div eID="gen17411" type="x-p"/>

entries.785c6f829940b7941bef6439ac3f040a130558f5: <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.4.1">Job 30:1-4   1</reference>  And now they who are younger than I have me in derision, <div eID="gen8157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8158" type="x-p"/> Those whose fathers I disdained To set with the dogs of my flock.   2  Yea, the strength of their hands, what should it profit me? <div eID="gen8158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8159" type="x-p"/> They have lost vigour and strength.   3  They are benumbed from want and hunger, <div eID="gen8159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> They who gnaw the steppe, <div eID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8161" type="x-p"/> The darkness of the wilderness and waste;   4  They who pluck mallows in the thicket, <div eID="gen8161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8162" type="x-p"/> And the root of the broom is their bread. <div eID="gen8162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8163" type="x-p"/> With ועתּה, which also elsewhere expresses the turning-point from the premises to the conclusion, from accusation to the threat of punishment, and such like, Job here begins to bewail the sad turn which his former prosperity has taken. The first line of the verse, which is marked off by <hi type="italic">Mercha-Mahpach,</hi> is intentionally so disproportionately long, to form a deep and long breathed beginning to the lamentation which is now begun. Formerly, as he has related in the first part of the monologue, an object of reverential fear to the respectable youth of the city (<reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>), he is now an object of derision (שׂחק על, to laugh at, distinct from שׂחק אל, <reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference>, to laugh to, smile upon) to the young good-for-nothing vagabonds of a miserable class of men. They are just the same עניּי ארץ, whose sorrowful lot he reckons among the mysteries of divine providence, so difficulty of solution (<reference osisRef="Job.24.4-Job.24.8">Job 24:4-8</reference>). The less he belongs to the merciless ones, who take advantage of the calamities of the poor for their own selfish ends, instead of relieving their distress as far as is in their power, the more unjustifiable is the rude treatment which he now experiences from them, when they who meanly hated him before because he was rich, now rejoice at the destruction of his prosperity.
