Hahn and Loch-Reischl rightly take אם in the sense of <hi type="italic">an</hi>. It introduces another turn of the question: Does one, however, not stretch out one’s hand to hasten the fall, or in his downfall (raise) a cry for help, or a wail, on that account? Döderlein’s conjecture, לחן for להן (praying “for favour”), deserves respectful mention, but it is not needed: להן signifies neutrally: in (under) such circumstances (comp. בּהם, <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa 64:5</reference>), or is directly equivalent to להן, which (Rth 1:13) signifies <hi type="italic">propterea</hi>, and even in biblical Chaldee, beside the Chaldee signif. <hi type="italic">sed , nisi ,</hi> retains this Hebrew signif. (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.6">Dan 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.9">Dan 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.24">Dan 4:24</reference>). פּיד, which signifies dying and destruction (Talmud. in the peculiar signif.: that which is hewn or pecked open), synon. of איד, has been already discussed on Job 12:5.
entries.eac4051a9982fca93e755c840e47ddab457609bd: <reference osisRef="Job.30.28-Job.31.28">Job 30:28-31 28</reference>  I wandered about in mourning without the sun; <div eID="gen8228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8229" type="x-p"/> I rose in the assembly, I gave free course to my complaint. 29  I am become a brother of the jackals <div eID="gen8229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8230" type="x-p"/> And a companion of ostriches. 30  My skin having become black, peels off from me, <div eID="gen8230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8231" type="x-p"/> And my bones are parched with dryness. 31  My harp was turned to mourning, <div eID="gen8231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8232" type="x-p"/> And my pipe to tones of sorrow. <div eID="gen8232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8233" type="x-p"/> Several expositors (Umbr., Vaih., Hlgst.) understand קדר of the dirty-black skin of the leper, but contrary to the usage of the language, according to which, in similar utterances (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.7">Psa 38:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Psa 42:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>, comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">Job 5:11</reference>), it rather denotes the dirty-black dress of mourners (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">qḏḏr , conspurcare vestem</hi>); to understand it of the dirty-black skin as <hi type="italic">quasi sordida veste</hi> (Welte) is inadmissible, since this distortion of the skin which Job bewails in <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">Job 30:30</reference> would hardly be spoken of thus tautologically. קדר therefore means in the black of the שׂק, or mourning-linen, <reference osisRef="Job.16.15">Job 16:15</reference>, by which, however, also the interpretation of בּלא חמּה, “without sunburn” (Ew., Hirz.), which has gained ground since Raschi’s day (לא שׁשׁזפתני השׁמשׁ), is disposed of; for “one can perhaps say of the blackness of the skin that it does not proceed from the sun, but not of the blackness of mourning attire” (Hahn). קדר also refutes the reading בלא חמה in lxx <hi type="italic">Complut</hi>. (ἄνευ θυμοῦ),<note placement="foot">Whereas <hi type="italic">Codd. Alex., Vat.,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sinait.,</hi> ἄνευ φιμοῦ, which is correctly explained by κημοῦ in Zwingli’s <hi type="italic">Aldine,</hi> but gives no sense.</note> <div eID="gen8233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8234" type="x-p"/> Syr., Jer. (<hi type="italic">sine furore</hi>), which ought to be understood of the deposition of the gall-pigment on the skin, and therefore of jaundice, which turns it (especially in tropical regions) not merely yellow, but a dark-brown. Hahn and a few others render בלא חמה correctly in the sense of בחשׁך, "without the sun having shone on him.” Bereft of all his possessions, and finally also of his children, he wanders about in mourning (הלּך as <reference osisRef="Job.24.10">Job 24:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.7">Psa 38:7</reference>), and even the sun had clothed itself in black to him (which is what קדר השׁמשׁ means, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference> and freq.); the celestial light, which otherwise brightened his path, <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference>, was become invisible. We must not forget that Job here reviews the whole chain of afflictions which have come upon him, so that by <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.30.28">Job 30:28</reference></hi> we have not to think exclusively, and also not prominently, of the leprosy, since הלכתי indeed represents him as still able to move about freely. <div eID="gen8234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8235" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.30.28">Job 30:28</reference></hi> the accentuation wavers between <hi type="italic">Dechî, Munach, Silluk,</hi> according to which בּקּהל אשׁוּע belong together, which is favoured by the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Tarcha, Munach, Silluk,</hi> according to which (because <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, according to <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 503, §2, is a transformation of <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch</hi>) קמתּי בּקּהל belong together. The latter mode of accentuation, according to which בקהל must be written without the <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. instead of בּקהל (vid., Norzi), is the only correct one (because <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> cannot come in the last member of the sentence before <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>), and is also more pleasing as to matter: I rose (and stood) in the assembly, crying for help, or more generally: wailing. The assembly is not to be thought of as an assembly of the people, or even tribunal (Ew.: ”before the tribunal seeking a judge, with lamentations”), but as the public; for the thought that Job sought help against his unmerited sufferings before a human tribunal is absurd; and, moreover, the thought that he cried for help before an assembly of the people called together to take counsel and pronounce decisions is equally absurd. Welte, however, who interprets: I was as one who, before an assembled tribunal, etc., introduces a <hi type="italic">quasi</hi> of which there is no trace in the text. בּקּהל must therefore, without pressing it further, be taken in the sense of <hi type="italic">publice</hi>, before all the world (Hirz.: comp. בקהל, ἐν φανερῷ, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">Pro 26:26</reference>); אשׁוּע, however, is a circumstantial clause declaring the purpose (Ew. §337, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; comp. De Sacy, <hi type="italic">Gramm. Arabe</hi> ii. §357), as is frequently the case after קום, <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11">Psa 88:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">Psa 102:14</reference> : <hi type="italic">surrexi in publico ut lamentarer,</hi> or <hi type="italic">lamentaturus,</hi> or <hi type="italic">lamentando.</hi> In this lament, extorted by the most intense pain, which he cannot hold back, however many may surround him, he is become a brother of those תּנּים, jackals (<hi type="italic">canes aurei</hi>), whose dolorous howling produces dejection and shuddering in all who hear it, and a companion of בּנות יענה, whose shrill cry is varied by wailing tones of deep melancholy.<note placement="foot">It is worth while to cite a passage from Shaw’s <hi type="italic">Travels in Barbary</hi>, ii. 348 (transl.), here: “When the ostriches are running and fighting, they sometimes make a wild, hideous, hissing noise with their throats distended and beaks open; at another time, if they meet with a slight opposition, they have a clucking or cackling voice like our domestic fowls: they seem to rejoice and laugh at the terror of their adversary. During the loneliness of the night however, as if their voice had a totally different tone, they often set up a dolorous, hideous moan, which at one time resembles the roar of the lion, and at another is more like the hoarser voice of other quadrupeds, especially the bull and cow. I have often heard them groan as if they were in the greatest agonies.” In General Doumas’ book on the <hi type="italic">Horse of the Sahara,</hi> I have read that the male ostrich (<hi type="italic">delı̂m</hi>), when it is killed, especially if its young ones are near, sends forth a dolorous note, wile the female (<hi type="italic">remda</hi>), on the other hand, does not utter a sound; and so, when the ostrich digs out its nest, one hears a languishing and dolorous tone all day long, and when it has laid its egg, its usual cry is again heard, only about three o'clock in the afternoon.</note> <div eID="gen8235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8236" type="x-p"/> The point of comparison is not the insensibility of the hearers (<hi type="italic">Sforno</hi>), but the fellowship of wailing and howling together with the accompanying idea of the desert in which it is heard, which is connected with the idea itself (comp. Mic 1:8).

                  <ns0:p n="24">24. Howbeit he will not stretch out <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hand to the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> heap.</ns0:note> grave, though they cry in his destruction <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">There is great variety and difficulty in the sense and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nexion of these words: They may be joyned either 1. with the following Verse, as describing <ns0:hi>Iob's</ns0:hi> compassion to others in affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction, which by the Principles of Reason and Religion should have procured him some pity from God and men in his affliction. And to that purpose the words are or may be translated thus; <ns0:hi>But</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>not</ns0:hi> my <ns0:hi>prayers</ns0:hi> for them (which words may be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood out of the following Clause) when <ns0:hi>he stretched out his hand?</ns0:hi> (to wit, against them to destroy them) <ns0:hi>in his destruction</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression</ns0:hi> (understand it actively, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> when God was about to destroy any other man or men) was not (the Negation being under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood out of the former Branch of the Verse, as is usual) my <ns0:hi>cry for them?</ns0:hi> the Feminine Gender being put for the Masculine, as it is elsewhere; or <ns0:hi>for these things,</ns0:hi> the Feminine being put for the Neuter; that is, for those destructive Calamities which were upon them? Or 2. with the foregoing Verse. And so these words contain either 1. a Consolation against the evil last mentioned: So the sense is, Though God will undoubtedly bring me to the Grave by these Torments, yet this comforts me, that <ns0:hi>surely he will not stretch out his hand</ns0:hi> (to wit, to afflict or punish me further, as this phrase is used. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 3. 20. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 9. 12, 13.) <ns0:hi>in the grave, though they, i. e.</ns0:hi> the perishing persons <ns0:hi>cry</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>roar (i. e.</ns0:hi> be sorely pained and tormented) <ns0:hi>in his destruction, i. e.</ns0:hi> whilest God is destroying them. Or this last Clause may be read interrogatively, <ns0:hi>Is there any cry in his destruction?</ns0:hi> When a man is cut off or destroyed by death, doth he then cry and complain? No, there is an end of all these Miseries. Or rather 2 a Confirmation of what he last said. For the whole Context shews that <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> is not taking any comfort to himself, but rather aggravating his Sufferings. I know, saith he, that I am a dead man, and my Condition is desperate, for <ns0:hi>surely he, i. e.</ns0:hi> God, <ns0:hi>will not stretch out his hand</ns0:hi> (to wit, to save or rescue me, as this phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 18 17. & 144. 7. compared with <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 4. 30.) <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in the grave (i. e.</ns0:hi> to a dead man, such as I am in effect, having not only one foot, but in a manner both feet in the grave, as being upon the very brink of the Pit) <ns0:hi>though they cry</ns0:hi> (to wit, unto God, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> though there be a great and a general Cry and Lamentation for him among his Friends or others, and an earnest desire of him, if possibly he might be restored to life again) <ns0:hi>in his destruction, i. e.</ns0:hi> when he is destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed or dead; yet all these Cries would be in vain.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:411" />25. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 35. 13, 14. Rom. 12. 15.</ns0:note> Did not I weep <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> for him that was hard of day.</ns0:note> for him that was in trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Whence is it that neither God nor man shew any compassion to me, but both conspire to afflict me and encrease my torments? Doth God now mete out to me the same measure which I meted out to others? Have I now Judgment without Mercy, because I afforded no mercy nor pity to others in misery? No, my Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />science acquits me from this inhumanity: I did not sleightly re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent, but bitterly mourn and weep over others in their miseries; and therefore I had reason to expect more Compassion than I find.</ns0:note>? was <ns0:hi>not</ns0:hi> my soul grieved for the poor <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Even for him who was not capable of requiting my kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness in case of his recovery: which shews that my sympathy was real, and not seigned, as it is in some who pretend great sorrow for the rich in their troubles, hoping thereby to insinuate them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves into their favour and friendship, and thereby to procure some advantage to themselves.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. When I looked for good, then evil came <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to me</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Instead of the return of the like pity to me, which I might justly challenge and expect whensoever I should stand in need of it, I meet with a sad disappointment, and my pity is recompensed with others cruelty to me.</ns0:note>: and when I waited for light, there came darkness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. My bowels boiled and rested not <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> My inward parts boyled without ceasing. The Bowels are the seat of Passion and of Compassion; and therefore this may be understood, either 1. of his Compassionate and deep sense of others miseries; which is oft expressed by <ns0:hi>bowels,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 16. 11. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3. 12. and elsewhere, of which he spake <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. to which he sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyns the contrary usage which he met with, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 26. And then in this first part of <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. he renews the mention of his compassion to others, and in the latter part he adds by way of Antithesis or Opposition, that his mercy was requited with cruel afflictions. Or 2. of the grievousness of his troubles, which is sometimes ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed by the troubling or boyling of the Bowels or inward parts; as <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 1. 20.</ns0:note>: the days of affliction prevented me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Came upon me suddenly and unexpected<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, when I promised to my self peace and prosperity, as the u<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sual recompence which God promiseth and giveth to such as fear and please him, as I have done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 38. 6. & 42. 9. & 43. 2.</ns0:note> I went <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>I walked</ns0:hi> hither and thither as I could. Or, <ns0:hi>I converse</ns0:hi> or appear among others.</ns0:note> mourning without the Sun <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Spending my days in mourning without any Sun-light or comfort; or so oppressed with sadness, that I did not care nor desire to see the light of the Sun. Heb. <ns0:hi>black not by the Sun.</ns0:hi> My very Countenance is changed and become black, but not by the Sun, which makes many other persons black; <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 1. 5. 6. but by the force of my Disease and deep Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lancholy which oft-times makes a man's Visage black and dismal. See <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 119. 83. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 5. 10. And this he repeats in plainer terms, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. as an eminent token of his excessive grief and mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sery.</ns0:note>: I stood up <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either because my Disease and pain made me weary of other postures: Or that others might take notice of me and be moved with pity towards me.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> I cried <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">With a loud and d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eful cla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mour through great and sudden anguish</ns0:note> in the congregation <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Where prudence and modesty taught me to forbear it, if extream necessity and misery had not forced me to it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 102. 6.</ns0:note> I am a brother <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, by imitation of their cries: Persons of like quali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties are oft called <ns0:hi>brethren,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 3. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 18. 9.</ns0:note> to dragons <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which howl and wail mournfully in the Deserts, <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. either through hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger or thirst, or when he fights with and is beaten by the Ele<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phant.</ns0:note>, and a com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />panion to <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Ostriches. Mic.</ns0:hi> 1. 8.</ns0:note> owls <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whose sad and mournful noises are known. Or <ns0:hi>Ostri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches,</ns0:hi> which also is noted to make lamentable out-cries.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
